claims.text: Premelting onset and overall melting behavior in HEA nanoparticles are governed primarily by surface composition heterogeneity.
Post-synthesis thermal annealing causes lower-melting-point elements to segregate to HEA nanoparticle surfaces.
Surface-segregated lower-melting-point elements act as nucleation sites for melting.
Surface segregation of lower-melting-point elements lowers the melting temperature relative to compositionally homogeneous nanoparticles.
Rapid thermal-shock synthesis can produce HEA-CoxMoyFe10Ni10Cu10 nanoparticles with homogeneous elemental distributions and without elemental segregation or phase separation.
Annealing-induced surface enrichment of lower-melting-point elements locally reduces cohesive energy.
Thermal annealing promotes diffusion of lower-melting-point elements to nanoparticle surfaces.
The lower cohesive contribution and less favorable metallic bonding of a constituent can favor its surface segregation.
Reduced local binding energy at a segregated surface facilitates premelting nucleation.
Annealed nanoparticles with segregated surfaces will show a lower premelting-onset temperature than homogeneous as-synthesized nanoparticles.
Annealed nanoparticles with segregated surfaces will exhibit a broader melting transition than homogeneous as-synthesized nanoparticles.
Homogeneously composed HEA nanoparticles are expected to display higher and sharper melting transitions.
The proposed behavior should hold when at least one HEA component has a significantly lower melting point and sufficient atomic mobility exists for surface segregation during annealing.
Systems whose composition or synthesis conditions already cause segregation may fall outside the proposed regime.
The magnitude of the melting-onset shift depends on elemental composition and annealing parameters.
Annealed and as-synthesized particles should be compared under identical heating rates and environmental conditions.
Premelting onset, complete melting, and surface composition before and after annealing are the proposed comparison measurements.

Failure to observe a statistically significant decrease in melting onset or a broader melting transition after confirmed surface segregation would falsify the proposed causal effect of segregation on melting.
